query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing that refines the coarse dual‐phase lamellar structure into an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure will simultaneously improve the strength and room-temperature ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies that contain numerous internal boundaries where microcracks can initiate under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled process involving cold-rolling (or another form of moderate plastic deformation) followed by optimized annealing to break down and refine the original coarse lamellar colonies.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile loading; processing must carefully balance deformation and annealing to avoid excessive coarsening (i.e., annealing must be controlled to maintain ultrafine structures).
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure featuring refined, hierarchical lamellar colonies with well-distributed internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Refinement produces a two-hierarchical constraint effect where the increased density of phase boundaries both impedes dislocation motion (strengthening) and provides effective sites for arresting microcracks (enhancing ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse lamellar alloy, the processed alloy will exhibit higher tensile strength and improved tensile ductility at room temperature due to the dual benefits of grain-boundary strengthening and enhanced microcrack resistance.
generation.baseline: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy produced by standard casting methods, yielding coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for eutectic high-entropy systems (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) when processing conditions are optimized to prevent over-annealing; its benefits may diminish if the processing parameters lead to excessive grain coarsening or loss of the lamellar morphology.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of deformation and exact annealing temperature/time required to achieve the optimal ultrafine structure is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition; scalability and potential trade-offs at different processing scales also warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of EHEA samples: one using conventional casting (baseline) and one undergoing tailored thermo-mechanical processing (cold rolling followed by optimized annealing). Perform room-temperature tensile tests and conduct microstructural characterization using electron microscopy to assess grain size, lamellar colony refinement, and crack propagation behavior.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure
Electron microscopy imaging for quantifying grain and lamellar sizes, as well as crack initiation and propagation patterns
Statistical comparison of mechanical properties between processed and unprocessed samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if excessive microcracking occurs earlier than in the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
